title: Camp 2 close: the cloud of witnesses (Hebrews 12:1)
hook: the saints aren't statues but a crowd cheering you on
carry: so great a cloud of witnesses
tomorrow: First Mass, or first in years

segments.voice: Yesterday, Teresa of Kolkata, at Nirmal Hriday through years of darkness. Your line was small things with great love. The stories end today.

The last mile of a marathon. The legs are gone and the lungs are burning. Then the runner turns a corner, and both sides of the street are packed. Strangers, shouting the name on the bib. Some ran this race last year; some ran it decades ago. They know this mile, and they're yelling: keep going, nearly there. An early Christian writer used a picture much like it in the Letter to the Hebrews. It's the picture Catholics have in mind when they look at a church full of saints. Not statues. A crowd.
screen: `THE LAST MILE.` → `BOTH SIDES OF THE STREET, PACKED.` → `NOT STATUES. A CROWD.`

segments.voice: Hebrews chapter eleven is a roll call of people who kept faith: Abel, Noah, Abraham and Sarah, Moses, Rahab, and many more the writer runs out of time to name. Then chapter twelve turns to the reader. In the Douay-Rheims: "having so great a cloud of witnesses over our head," let us lay down every weight and run the race. A cloud, not a handful. The Greek word for witness is martys, which later gave us martyr: witnesses who have finished, watching the ones still running. In the Apostles' Creed, said at baptisms and at the start of the rosary, Catholics say they believe in the communion of saints: the Church as one family across death. Catholics speak of it in three parts: those still on earth, those being made ready for God, and those already with God in heaven. Love goes across all three. That's why Catholics pray for the dead, and ask the saints to pray for them, the way you'd ask a friend. Think back over this camp. Two pregnant women meeting in the hill country, and a child with no room at the inn. Fishermen, a woman at a well, a man through a roof, a lost son, a Samaritan on the road. A garden, a cross, an empty tomb, a road to Emmaus. Fire at Pentecost. Mary. Then the saints: Augustine, Patrick, Clare, Catherine, Joan, More, Bernadette, Thérèse, Kolbe, Teresa. Seventy-five days of stories. Catholics would say that's not a list of the dead. That's the crowd on the street.
screen: `A ROLL CALL IN HEBREWS ELEVEN.` · `A CLOUD OF WITNESSES, WATCHING.` · `ONE FAMILY ACROSS DEATH.` · `SEVENTY-FIVE DAYS OF STORIES.` · then, large: `SO GREAT A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.`

segments.voice: Let one face from this camp's stories come forward: the one who surprised you, maybe, or the one most like you, or least. Don't choose the most impressive; choose the one you'd want beside you on a bad day, a saint to walk with this year, and say their name once, quietly. If you pray, you can ask them to pray for you.
communio sanctorum. Latin for the communion of saints, the Church as one family across death, in prayer for each other.
Your line: so great a cloud of witnesses. Tomorrow Camp Three, the practices, starts at the church door. That's Camp Two, done.

howItsDone: Catholics profess the communion of saints in the Apostles' Creed, pray for the dead especially in November and on All Souls' Day, keep All Saints' Day on November 1, and often choose a patron saint at baptism or confirmation.

what it means: the whole Church is one family across death, and the ones who finished are cheering on the ones still running.
what a scholar hears: nephos martyrōn, a cloud of witnesses, and martys is the root of martyr. the creed's phrase can mean both holy people and holy things shared.
recall: British-born bishop who went to Ireland

chat.says: Why do Catholics ask saints to pray for them? Aren't the saints dead?
options: Catholics see the Church as one family across death, so they ask saints, like asking a friend.
Only martyrs are counted as saints, so Catholics ask the martyrs alone.
Catholics only study the saints' lives; asking them to pray isn't part of it.
chat.meaning: In the communion of saints, love goes across death. So Catholics ask the saints to pray for them, the way you'd ask a friend.
